title: Demonstrate a bug caused by using a shared mutable `ArrayList` inside `forEach` of a parallel stream (race condition).
shortTitle: Demonstrate a bug caused by a shared mutable ArrayList inside forEach of a parallel stream

s1_definition.profdef: Adding to a non-thread-safe `ArrayList` from `forEach` on a parallel stream is a race condition: multiple threads call `add` concurrently without synchronization, causing lost updates, nulls, or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
s1_definition.analogy: Several clerks write into the same ledger at once without taking turns. They overwrite each other's lines, leave blanks, or crash — the ledger ends up wrong.
s1_definition.oneliner: Parallel `forEach` adding to a shared `ArrayList` is a data race — results are corrupt or it throws.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Adding to a non-thread-safe `ArrayList` from `forEach` on a parallel stream is a race condition: multiple threads call `add` concurrently without synchronization, causing lost updates, nulls, or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Several clerks write into the same ledger at once without taking turns. They overwrite each other's lines, leave blanks, or crash — the ledger ends up wrong.

**One line to remember:** Parallel `forEach` adding to a shared `ArrayList` is a data race — results are corrupt or it throws.

sections.s2_technical:
`list.parallelStream().forEach(results::add)` has many threads calling `ArrayList.add` simultaneously. ArrayList is not thread-safe: add mutates a size field and an element array without locking, so concurrent adds interleave badly. The symptoms are non-deterministic — the result list ends up shorter than expected, contains nulls, or the internal array resize races and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

This is a classic misuse. The bug is intermittent, which makes it dangerous: it may pass in testing with small data and fail in production under load. The root cause is sharing mutable state across threads with no synchronization.

The senior nuance is that the fix is not to synchronize the add but to stop sharing mutable state — use `collect(Collectors.toList())`, which the stream framework manages thread-safely with per-thread accumulators merged at the end. Side-effecting into external collections from streams, especially parallel ones, violates the side-effect-free guideline precisely because of this race. Recognising the non-determinism as a data race is the key insight.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at the National Bank of India collected filtered transactions by adding to a shared ArrayList inside a parallel forEach, and the result list was intermittently short or corrupt.

This is exactly the parallel-forEach-shared-list race — the demo shows the corrupted counts.

The code defines a `BuggyCollectService demonstrating the race and a demo running it repeatedly.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: one hundred thousand integers, filtering the fifty thousand even ones.

Step 1: parallelStream splits the source across worker threads.

Step 2: Each thread filters its chunk and calls add on the same shared ArrayList.

Step 3: Concurrent adds race on the size field and internal array, so some writes are lost or overwrite each other.

Step 4: The returned list is often shorter than fifty thousand, may contain nulls, or the resize race throws an exception — and the outcome changes run to run.

```
WARNING: run 1 → size=48731 (expected 100000; race corrupts it)
SEVERE: run 2 → threw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
WARNING: run 3 → size=49122 (expected 100000; race corrupts it)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The bug is adding to a shared, non-thread-safe ArrayList from forEach on a parallel stream. ArrayList's add mutates its size field and its internal element array without any locking, so when many parallel worker threads call add at the same time their writes interleave badly. The symptoms are non-deterministic: the result list ends up shorter than expected, contains nulls, or the internal array resize races and throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

What makes this dangerous is that it is intermittent. With a small dataset in a unit test it often passes, because the work may not actually run in parallel or the race window is tiny, and then it fails in production under real load. At the National Bank of India this exact pattern produced a transaction list that was silently short on some runs.

The senior point I stress is that the correct fix is not to synchronize the add or wrap the list — it is to stop sharing mutable state entirely and use collect with a collector, which the stream framework manages safely with per-thread accumulators merged at the end. Side-effecting into an external collection from any stream, and especially a parallel one, violates the side-effect-free guideline precisely because it invites this data race. Naming the non-determinism as a data race on shared mutable state is the insight an interviewer is listening for.
